caveats:
The area of interest is the observed flood extent of 27 August 2026 widened by 200
metres. The flood extent is an interpretation of imagery for a single date rather than
a surveyed boundary, and water levels changed through the event.

OpenStreetMap coverage reflects where volunteer mappers have been active and changes
between updates. Overture layers combine several upstream sources, some of them machine
generated. Cross-check critical decisions with local field knowledge.
dataset_source: OpenStreetMap contributors, Overture Maps, volunteer field reports
name: hot_flood_npl
notes:
OpenStreetMap and Overture Maps vector layers for the area flooded in the 2026 Bhote
Koshi and Trishuli flood, Nepal, and the ground immediately around it.

The area of interest is the observed flood extent of 27 August 2026 widened by 200
metres, 90.11 square kilometres in total. The flood extent was mapped from drone,
Landsat, PlanetScope and Sentinel imagery and covers 31.70 square kilometres. It is
published here as its own resource, so the water line can be separated from the margin
around it.

The 200 m margin includes buildings and roads next to the water, not only those in it.
Being in this dataset does not mean a feature was flooded. Use the Flood Extent resource
for the water only.

The extent spans Bagmati and Gandaki Provinces, five districts, Rasuwa, Nuwakot,
Dhading, Gorkha and Chitawan, and sixteen municipalities, following the river from
Rasuwagadhi to the Narayani confluence.

Presence in this dataset does not by itself mean a feature was damaged or destroyed.

Buildings mappers have recorded as destroyed are in a separate **Destroyed Buildings**
layer. The `destroyed:` prefix replaces the plain `building` tag, so these are not in the
Buildings layer. Read both together for the building stock before the flood.

AI-scored building damage from post-event imagery is published separately as [Nepal
Flood 2026: fAIr Damage Assessment](https://data.humdata.org/dataset/hot_flood_npl_buildings_damage).

This is the close view, the flooded ground and a 200 m margin. **For the wider
1 km river corridor under assessment, 317 sq km from Rasuwagadhi to the Narayani
confluence, use [Nepal Flood 2026 River
Corridor](https://data.humdata.org/dataset/hot_flood_npl_corridor).**

Every layer is published here as a resource, and most layers carry two versions, one
from OpenStreetMap and one from Overture Maps. The two are not interchangeable:

- **OpenStreetMap** layers are live. They are rebuilt every six hours, and each rebuild queries
  OpenStreetMap directly rather than reading a pre-cut country extract, so a layer
  reflects the map as it stood minutes before the file was written. Work done by
  volunteer mappers during the response shows up in the next rebuild. Use these when
  currency matters.
- **Overture Maps** layers fuse building footprints and other features from Microsoft,
  Google and OpenStreetMap. That fusion gives broader coverage than OSM alone in places
  volunteers have not reached yet, but **Overture is not updated daily**. It follows
  Overture's own release cycle, so it will not reflect mapping done during this response
  and will fall progressively further behind the OpenStreetMap layers.

In short, Overture is wider but older; OpenStreetMap is current. For damage assessment
against the latest mapping, prefer the OpenStreetMap layers and treat Overture as a
supplement where OSM coverage is thin.

Mapping task boundaries from the Tasking Manager campaign are published here too and
refreshed daily, showing where volunteers are being asked to map.

The bridge damage assessment is reported from the ground by volunteers. It lists road
bridges with their condition after the flood, deck length where measured, and
administrative codes from the same boundaries as the other layers.

- Source: [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/), [Overture Maps](https://overturemaps.org/), volunteer field reports
- Part of HOT disaster response exports on HDX by [HOT](https://www.hotosm.org/)

Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team (HOT) acts as a bridge between the traditional humanitarian responders and the OpenStreetMap Community. HOT works both remotely and physically in countries to assist the collection of geographic data, usage of that information and training others in OpenStreetMap.

resources.description: Mapping task boundaries for the Tasking Manager campaign "2026 Nepal Floods". 4 project(s) covering 532 sq km, 69% mapped on average, 369 contributor(s) to date. Status included: ARCHIVED, PUBLISHED. Each feature is one Tasking Manager project boundary and carries its id, name, status, priority, organisation, mapping types, completion percentages, contributor counts and a link to the project. This layer shows where volunteers are being asked to map, which is not the same as where data exists: a project at low completion marks a known gap rather than coverage. Regenerated daily from the Tasking Manager API, so the percentages track live progress. Source: HOT Tasking Manager (https://tasks.hotosm.org/).
